questions.subject: CN
questions.question: Which protocol is connection-oriented?
questions.explanation: TCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake before sending data. UDP, IP and ICMP are connectionless.
questions.hint: TCP = Telephone call (connect first). UDP = posting a letter.
questions.trap: IP is part of TCP/IP, but IP itself is connectionless.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: What is the default port number of HTTPS?
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TCP port 443. Plain HTTP uses port 80.
questions.trap: 80 is HTTP (not secure); 8080 is only a common alternative for HTTP.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: Which OSI layer decides the route between different networks?
questions.explanation: The network layer (layer 3) handles logical (IP) addressing and routing. Routers work here.
questions.trap: The data link layer moves frames only within one network, using MAC addresses.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: DNS queries normally travel over which transport protocol?
questions.explanation: Normal DNS lookups use UDP port 53 because they are small and fast. TCP port 53 is used for zone transfers and very large replies.
questions.hint: DNS asks a quick question: UDP.
questions.trap: Many pick TCP because DNS "can" use TCP; the normal query is UDP.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: How many usable host addresses does a /24 IPv4 subnet have?
questions.explanation: A /24 leaves 8 host bits: 2^8 = 256 addresses. Two are reserved (network and broadcast), so 254 are usable.
questions.trap: 256 counts the network and broadcast addresses too.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: What does ARP find?
options: The MAC address for a known IP address
The IP address for a known MAC address
The IP address of a domain name
questions.answer: The MAC address for a known IP address
questions.explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) asks the local network "who has this IP?" and gets back the MAC address.
questions.trap: Finding the IP from a MAC was RARP, the reverse. Domain to IP is DNS.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: Which device forwards frames using MAC addresses?
questions.explanation: A switch works at the data link layer and sends each frame only to the port with the matching MAC address.
questions.hint: Switch = smart, sends to one port. Hub = shouts to all.
questions.trap: A router uses IP addresses (layer 3), not MAC addresses.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits. IPv4 is 32 bits.
questions.trap: 48 bits is the length of a MAC address.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: In which topology is every device connected to one central device?
questions.explanation: In a star topology each node has its own cable to a central hub or switch. If the centre fails, the whole network stops.
questions.trap: Mesh connects devices to each other, not to one centre.

questions.subject: CN
questions.question: Which protocol sends email from one mail server to another?
questions.explanation: SMTP sends (pushes) mail. POP3 and IMAP are used by your app to read (pull) mail from the server.
questions.trap: SNMP manages network devices; it has nothing to do with email.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: Which gates are called universal gates?
questions.explanation: Any logic circuit can be built using only NAND gates, or only NOR gates.
questions.hint: NAND and NOR: the "N" gates can do aNything.
questions.trap: XOR and XNOR are special-purpose gates, not universal.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: What is binary 1011 in decimal?
questions.trap: 13 is 1101: same digits in a different order.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: How many bits can one flip-flop store?
questions.explanation: A flip-flop is the basic 1-bit memory cell: its output is either 0 or 1.
questions.trap: A register of 8 flip-flops stores 8 bits.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: What is the 2's complement of 0101 (4 bits)?
questions.explanation: Invert every bit (0101 → 1010), then add 1: 1010 + 1 = 1011.
questions.hint: Flip the bits, then add one.
questions.trap: 1010 is only the 1's complement.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: When is the output of a 2-input XOR gate 1?
options: When the inputs are the same
questions.explanation: XOR is the "odd one out" gate: output 1 when exactly one input is 1.
questions.hint: XOR = eXclusive: one or the other, not both.
questions.trap: "Inputs the same" describes XNOR.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: How many address lines does the 8085 microprocessor have?
questions.explanation: The 8085 has 16 address lines, so it can address 2^16 = 64 KB of memory. Its data bus is 8 bits.
questions.trap: 20 address lines belongs to the 8086 (1 MB).

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: How many select lines does an 8-to-1 multiplexer need?
questions.explanation: Select lines n satisfy 2^n = number of inputs. 2^3 = 8, so 3 select lines.
questions.trap: 8 is the number of data inputs, not select lines.

questions.subject: DE
questions.question: Which flip-flop toggles its output when both of its inputs are 1?
questions.explanation: In a JK flip-flop, J = K = 1 makes the output toggle. In an SR flip-flop, S = R = 1 is not allowed.
questions.trap: The T flip-flop also toggles, but it has only one input (T).

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: In amplitude modulation (AM), the message changes which property of the carrier?
questions.explanation: In AM the carrier's amplitude follows the message signal; its frequency stays constant.
questions.trap: Frequency change is FM; phase change is PM.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: What is the Nyquist rate for a signal whose highest frequency is 4 kHz?
questions.explanation: Nyquist rate = 2 × highest frequency = 2 × 4 kHz = 8 kHz.
questions.hint: Sample at least twice the top frequency.
questions.trap: 4 kHz is the signal frequency itself; sampling at that rate causes aliasing.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: What is the bandwidth of standard AM (DSB-FC) for a message of bandwidth fm?
questions.explanation: AM produces an upper and a lower sideband, each fm wide, so total bandwidth = 2fm.
questions.trap: fm is the bandwidth of SSB, which keeps only one sideband.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: Which modulation is better at rejecting amplitude noise?
questions.explanation: Noise mostly changes amplitude. FM carries the message in frequency, so the receiver can clip amplitude changes away.
questions.trap: DSB-SC and SSB are still amplitude modulation, so they suffer like AM.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: Light travels along an optical fibre by:
questions.explanation: Light hits the core-cladding boundary above the critical angle and is totally reflected back into the core.
questions.trap: Refraction happens when light enters the fibre, but it is not what guides it.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: GSM 900 operates in which frequency band?
questions.explanation: UHF covers 300 MHz to 3 GHz, which includes 900 MHz.
questions.trap: VHF ends at 300 MHz; SHF starts at 3 GHz.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: What is the Shannon channel capacity formula?
questions.explanation: Shannon: C = B log2(1 + S/N) bits per second, with B in Hz and S/N as a plain ratio (not dB).
questions.trap: The "2B" belongs to Nyquist's noiseless formula C = 2B log2 M.

questions.subject: COM
questions.question: In PCM, adding one more bit per sample improves the signal-to-quantisation noise ratio by about:
questions.explanation: SQNR ≈ 1.76 + 6.02n dB, so each extra bit adds about 6 dB.
questions.trap: 3 dB means doubling power, which is a different rule.

questions.subject: EDC
questions.question: What is the cut-in (knee) voltage of a silicon diode?
questions.explanation: A silicon diode starts conducting at about 0.7 V. A germanium diode needs about 0.3 V.
questions.trap: 0.3 V is germanium, a common swap in exams.

questions.subject: EDC
questions.question: Which equation is Ohm's law?
questions.explanation: Voltage across a resistor equals current times resistance.
questions.hint: "VIR": Virat is Royal. V = I × R.
questions.trap: I = V/R is the same law rearranged, but I = VR is wrong.

questions.subject: EDC
questions.question: Which BJT configuration gives the highest power gain?
questions.explanation: Common emitter has good current gain and voltage gain together, so its power gain is the highest.
questions.trap: Common collector (emitter follower) has voltage gain of about 1. Common drain is a FET circuit.

questions.subject: EDC
questions.question: Two 10 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: For two equal resistors in parallel, total = R/2 = 10/2 = 5 Ω.
questions.hint: Equal resistors in parallel: divide by how many.
questions.trap: 20 Ω is the series total.

questions.subject: EDC
questions.question: A Zener diode is mainly used as a:
questions.explanation: In reverse breakdown, a Zener keeps a nearly constant voltage across it, so it regulates voltage.
questions.trap: An ordinary PN diode is the rectifier.

questions.subject: EDC
questions.question: What is the input impedance of an ideal op-amp?
questions.explanation: An ideal op-amp draws no input current, so its input impedance is infinite. Its output impedance is zero.
questions.trap: Zero is the ideal OUTPUT impedance.

notes.subject: CN
notes.title: TCP vs UDP
notes.keyDifference: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and fast.
points: TCP: handshake, acknowledgements, resends lost data, keeps order. Header 20–60 bytes.
UDP: no handshake, no acknowledgements. Header 8 bytes.
TCP for web, email, file transfer. UDP for DNS, live video, games.
notes.memoryTrick: TCP = Telephone call. UDP = posting letters.
notes.examTrap: DNS normally uses UDP port 53, but TCP 53 for zone transfers.

notes.subject: CN
notes.title: Hub vs switch vs router
notes.keyDifference: Hub repeats to all ports (layer 1), switch uses MAC (layer 2), router uses IP (layer 3).
points: Hub: one collision domain, dumb repeater.
Switch: each port is its own collision domain.
Router: joins different networks and separates broadcast domains.
notes.memoryTrick: Hub shouts, switch whispers, router gives directions.
notes.examTrap: A switch does NOT separate broadcast domains; a router does.

notes.subject: DE
notes.title: Universal gates
notes.keyDifference: NAND and NOR can build every other gate.
points: NOT from NAND: tie both inputs together.
AND from NAND: NAND followed by NAND-as-NOT.

notes.subject: DE
notes.title: 1's vs 2's complement
notes.keyDifference: 1's complement flips bits; 2's complement flips bits and adds 1.
points: 2's complement has only one zero; 1's complement has +0 and -0.
notes.examTrap: For 4 bits the range is -8 to +7, not -7 to +7.

notes.subject: COM
notes.title: Nyquist rate vs Nyquist interval
notes.keyDifference: Nyquist rate = 2fm (samples per second); Nyquist interval = 1/(2fm) (time between samples).
points: Example: fm = 4 kHz gives rate 8 kHz and interval 125 µs.
notes.memoryTrick: Rate is a frequency, interval is a time.
notes.examTrap: Questions ask for the interval in µs to catch you giving the rate.

notes.subject: EDC
notes.title: Silicon vs germanium diode
points: Silicon has much lower leakage current and works at higher temperatures.
Germanium is used where a small forward drop matters.
notes.examTrap: Leakage (reverse saturation) current is higher in germanium, not silicon.
